fact: English is a West Germanic language whose vocabulary is more than half Latin and French in origin.
William Shakespeare is credited with introducing or popularising over 1,700 English words, among them 'lonely', 'swagger' and 'bedazzled'.
The oldest surviving English poem, 'Caedmon's Hymn', was composed in the 7th century.
English has no official academy; its usage is set by convention and dictionaries rather than by a regulator.
The letter 'e' is the most common letter in English, appearing in roughly one in nine words.
The dot over the letters 'i' and 'j' is called a 'tittle'.
'Dord' was a real dictionary ghost word, printed in Webster's 1934 edition by mistake.
The word 'alphabet' comes from the first two letters of the Greek alphabet, alpha and beta.
English is the third most spoken native language in the world, after Mandarin Chinese and Spanish.
The Great Vowel Shift, between roughly 1400 and 1700, changed how English long vowels were pronounced.
'Beowulf' is the longest surviving poem written in Old English.
English spelling often preserves medieval pronunciations, which is why 'knight' and 'through' look nothing like they sound.
The Oxford English Dictionary contains more than 500,000 entries and took almost 50 years to compile.
'OK' is among the most widely recognised words in the world and may be the most spoken word on Earth.
Samuel Johnson published his 'Dictionary of the English Language' in 1755.
English word order is subject-verb-object, and meaning often depends on order rather than on case endings.
English once had a distinct singular pronoun, 'thou', which fell out of everyday use by the 18th century.
The word 'sandwich' comes from the 4th Earl of Sandwich, said to have eaten meat between bread to keep playing cards.
English is the most widely taught second language in the world.
Words such as 'shampoo', 'bungalow' and 'pyjamas' entered English from Hindi and other Indian languages.
The term 'big bang' was coined by the astronomer Fred Hoyle, and 'quark' was borrowed from a James Joyce novel.
English uses the apostrophe to mark possession and contraction, a feature largely absent from related languages.
'Set' has one of the largest numbers of distinct dictionary meanings of any English word.
The first English dictionary, by Robert Cawdrey in 1604, defined only about 3,000 words.
The pronoun 'I' is the only English pronoun that is always capitalised.
Noah Webster's American dictionary of 1828 helped fix distinct American spellings such as 'color' and 'center'.
English has unusually many synonyms because it absorbed words from many languages, often with subtle differences of register.
The sentence 'the quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog' is a pangram: it uses every letter of the alphabet.
Old English looked so different from modern English that 'Beowulf' is usually read in translation.
The words 'beef', 'pork' and 'mutton' come from Norman French, while 'cow', 'pig' and 'sheep' are Anglo-Saxon.
English grammar once had a full case system and grammatical gender, both lost after the Norman Conquest.
'Rhythm' is one of the longest common English words written without the vowel letters a, e, i, o or u.
English is the working language of international air traffic control and maritime communication.
The playwright Christopher Marlowe helped establish blank verse, which Shakespeare then made his own.
The word 'goodbye' is a contraction of the old farewell 'God be with ye'.
English has borrowed words so freely from other languages that it is sometimes called a 'magpie' language.
Daniel Defoe's 'Robinson Crusoe', published in 1719, is often called one of the first English novels.
The letter 'z' is the least frequently used letter in English.
Many English plurals are irregular, such as 'child/children' and 'mouse/mice'.
Geoffrey Chaucer wrote 'The Canterbury Tales' in Middle English in the late 14th century.
The word 'nice' once meant 'foolish' or 'ignorant' before shifting to its modern sense of 'pleasant'.
